source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: A learned correctness estimate needs few graded examples: about 1000 labeled right/wrong cases beat the simpler baselines.
numbers: Fine-tuning on graded generations: about 1000 examples already beat baselines; gains keep coming, and marginal benefit shrinks after about 5000. Training set about 20,000 with 2000 held out for temperature scaling. Multiple-choice and open-ended MMLU; LLaMA-2 7B, Mistral 7B, Mistral 7B-Instruct.
quote: having around 1000 labeled examples is enough to improve performance over simpler baselines
limits: Nearest thing to a sample-size answer for gap 1: about 10^3 graded items for a learned estimator. It is not a hit-rate floor for a task class, and no sequential-testing threshold is given. Models were fine-tuned (LoRA), which a scaffold-only agent cannot do.
agent_relevance: Order-of-magnitude budget: a tracker that needs thousands of graded cases is not available early; expect deliberate mode for the first hundreds of cases of a class.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Sampling agreement was weak at telling right from wrong; verbalised confidence ranked better but was poorly calibrated; a trained correctness classifier beat both.
numbers: On MMLU (multiple choice and open-ended), sampling-based uncertainty (semantic clustering) gave good calibration but very weak discrimination. Verbal elicitation matched weaker fine-tuned methods in discrimination but had poor calibration even after temperature scaling. Exact AUROC values are in a figure and were not read.
quote: sampling methods can yield good calibration, their discriminative performance is very weak
limits: Closest direct comparison for gap 2 (outcome-trained estimator vs verbal vs sample agreement), but the trained estimator is a fine-tuned correctness model, not a simple per-class hit rate. Tokens were not equalised.
agent_relevance: Supports using outcome-graded history as the trust signal and treating sample agreement as the weakest discriminator on open-ended tasks. No per-class hit rate was tested at equal tokens, so gap 2 stays open.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: A correctness estimator learned on one format and subject mix carried over to new formats, new subjects, and other models' answers.
numbers: Subject shift: LoRA+Prompt estimator performed similarly across MMLU supercategories though training had almost no social-science items. Format shift: open-ended to multiple-choice transfer was easier than the reverse. Mistral 7B scored LLaMA-2 7B answers with better AUROC than LLaMA-2 7B scored its own. Coding appendix: 62 LeetCode-easy questions; calibration worsened for two of three models.
quote: Learned uncertainty estimates generalize to new formatting, subject matter, and even the generations of other models.
limits: Transfer tested inside exam-style QA; the coding test is tiny and mixed. It shows a trust signal can cross some shifts, not that the edge of a task class can be detected.
agent_relevance: Weak support that one external tracker could serve several task classes. For gap 10 it shows the opposite risk too: the tracker may not flag a shifted item.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: In a human-AI exam study, people used LLM confidence scores to decide when to rely on the model, but only when the scores were informative.
numbers: N = 181 participants did a multiple-choice exam with Mistral 7B Instruct. Reliance moved with informative confidence; a random-uniform confidence baseline did not move reliance. The biggest benefit went to the lowest-performing users, not average accuracy.
quote: Lower performing users are most improved by access to confidence scores.
limits: Preliminary, one model; authors say more work is needed to separate calibration from how humans use it.
agent_relevance: Not about an agent's own gating, but shows a calibrated external score changes decisions where a random one does not.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Replacing the labels in few-shot demonstrations with random labels barely hurt classification and multiple-choice accuracy, so models were not mainly learning the label mapping.
numbers: 12 models including the GPT-3 family, k = 16 demonstrations. Drop 0-5% absolute for random labels; 1.7% average in multi-choice, 2.6% in classification.
quote: replacing labels in the demonstrations barely hurts performance on a range of classification and multi-choice tasks
limits: 2022 models; classification and multiple choice only; the paper says trends depend on the dataset. Generation tasks differ (next line).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: noisy or wrong in-context labels may do little harm on easy classification, but this also means in-context outcomes may not teach the input-to-label relation. Keep the task-class track record outside the prompt, in the harness.

source: Gao et al. (2024) On the Noise Robustness of In-Context Learning for Text Generation
finding: On text-generation tasks, noisy demonstration labels hurt in-context learning clearly, unlike the classification result, and more demonstrations did not fix it.
numbers: Llama2-7B and others; noise injected into 20%, 40%, 60% of annotations. Higher noise gave lower exact match; irrelevant noise hurt more than relevant noise; K = 8 was generally worse than K = 2 under noise. Their ranking fix (LPR) raised EM by up to 18.75; its gain fell from 10.26 to 0.92 (TopK) as irrelevant noise rose from 60% to 90%.
quote: noisy annotations significantly hurt the performance of in-context learning on text generation
limits: Noise is random flipping or mismatch, not delayed or ambiguous outcome signals; small open model; QA-style generation. Delay is not tested at all.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: label noise matters for generative tasks, which is where an agent's own track record is also hardest to grade. Delay stays untested.

source: Atil et al. (2025) Non-Determinism of 'Deterministic' LLM Settings
finding: Even at temperature 0, five LLMs gave different outputs for the same input across 10 runs, so within-agent noise is real and depends on the task.
numbers: Five LLMs, eight tasks, 10 runs, zero-shot and few-shot. Accuracy varied up to 15% across runs; gap between best and worst possible accuracy up to 70%. No model repeated accuracy across all tasks. Raw-output agreement (TARr@10) was usually low; answer-level agreement (TARa@10) higher but far from perfect.
quote: none of the LLMs consistently delivers repeatable accuracy across all tasks
limits: Models are 2024-era (e.g. GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama-3-70B). This is zero-temperature infrastructure noise, not sampling noise at normal temperature, and decomposition is not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: the Noise-book problem exists in LLMs even without sampling. One run is one draw, so the trust test should use answer-level agreement and the harness should log run-to-run variation per task class.

source: Atil et al. (2025) Non-Determinism of 'Deterministic' LLM Settings
finding: Instability differed by task: navigation answers were repeatable, college math and professional accounting were scattered.
numbers: Few-shot setting. High TARa@10 on navigation; scattered TARa@10 on college math and professional accounting. Best-minus-worst accuracy gaps over 10 points often came with very low raw-output agreement.
quote: leaderboards on this task can be expected to be more reliable
limits: Benchmark tasks, not natural work. Correlational only.
agent_relevance: Within-agent noise is a property of the task class, so measure it per class (supports the task-class unit of trust, K07).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: In controlled puzzles, non-thinking models beat thinking models on low-complexity items, thinking helped at medium complexity, and both collapsed at high complexity.
numbers: Tunable-size puzzle environments; Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking vs non-thinking and DeepSeek-R1 vs V3, equal token budgets. Three regimes: low (non-thinking more accurate and token-efficient), medium (thinking better), high (both fail).
quote: low-complexity tasks where standard models surprisingly outperform LRMs
limits: Puzzle tasks, early-2025 models, not the implicit-pattern tasks of Liu et al. Published rebuttals argue some failures come from output limits or unsolvable instances; I did not open them, so the collapse point is contested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a per-complexity map exists for 2025-era models, and says direct mode wins on easy items. Complexity is not the same as K&K validity; no study maps frontier models by cue validity.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Near the collapse point, reasoning models reduced their thinking effort even with token budget left, and failed to use explicit algorithms reliably.
numbers: Reasoning tokens rose with complexity then fell past a critical point; models reasoned inconsistently across problem sizes.
quote: their reasoning effort increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines
agent_relevance: More deliberation is not a reliable fallback when an item is beyond the model; deliberate mode needs its own stop and escalation rule.

source: Rethinking the Role of Teams and Training in Geopolitical Forecasting: The Effect of Uncontrolled Method Variance on Statistical Conclusions (Psychological Science, 2025, ahead of print; abstract read on a journal-alert page)
finding: A 2025 item-response-theory reanalysis of the Mellers et al. 2014 tournament data found that the teaming and training effects shrank, vanished or even reversed once extraneous variables were controlled.
numbers: Latent ability modelled from forecasting choices; best-fit models across the first 2 years included extraneous variables. Latent traits tied to strategic responding could tell superforecasters from others, so the factors behind their skill were hard to name.
quote: extraneous variables substantially eliminated, reduced, and, in some cases, even reversed the effects
limits: Abstract only; author names and full methods not seen. It challenges the 2014 team and training effects, not clearly the persistence of superforecaster skill. A persistence figure of about 0.65 year to year came from a secondary summary and was not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly answered: K10 (training and teaming about 10% each) should be marked contested. Persistence of top-forecaster skill is a separate claim that this abstract neither confirms nor refutes.

source: Atanasov & Himmelstein (2023) Talent Spotting in Crowd Prediction, in Judgment in Predictive Analytics (Springer, ch. 6)
finding: Skill measures that do not use accuracy correlate with outcomes at a median r of about 0.20; when accuracy is unavailable, peer-rating and behavioural measures do best.
numbers: Five groups of measures compared on one dataset: accuracy, intersubjective (peer rating, similarity), behaviours (activity, updating, coherence, rationale language), traits (cognitive reflection, numeracy), expertise (knowledge, calibration, self-rated expertise). LASSO selection agrees.
quote: individual, persistent skill in crowd prediction
limits: Abstract only (full text unavailable). Persistence is background in the abstract, not tested there.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: when no outcome is known yet, proxies exist for who is skilled, but they are weak (r about 0.20). Proxies for task validity itself were not found.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) R-Tuning: Instructing Large Language Models to Say 'I Don't Know' (NAACL 2024)
finding: Tuning a model on data split into questions it knows and does not know taught it to refuse out-of-knowledge items, and the refusal skill carried to out-of-domain datasets.
numbers: ParaRel and MMLU; OpenLLaMA-3B, LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-13B; in-domain and out-of-domain settings; average-precision (AP) of refusal-aware answering was mostly higher than the vanilla model. The table text extracted garbled, so per-cell values are not recorded.
quote: refusal ability was found to be a meta-skill that could be generalized to other tasks
limits: Fine-tuning, small LLaMA models, factual QA. Over-refusal cost not reported in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: an agent can learn a general 'outside what I know' signal, but that took training; a scaffold-only agent has only sampling disagreement and external track records.

source: Wen et al. (2024) Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
finding: The abstention survey says models do not learn why they should abstain, so abstention generalises poorly to out-of-distribution queries, and helpfulness and abstention conflict.
numbers: Survey across query, model and human-value views. It reports fully fine-tuned models over-refuse while LoRA reduces this (citing Brahman et al. 2024). No pooled false-alarm cost figure.
quote: LLMs lack understanding of the reasons behind abstention
limits: Survey; cited findings are second-hand, and I read only its discussion text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: over-refusal is named as a risk but not measured in a form an agent can use. Set the out-of-class alarm threshold by cost in the harness, not by the model.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Few-shot demonstrations help mainly by showing the format, the input distribution and the label space; removing the input-label format erased the gain.
numbers: Replacing in-distribution inputs with out-of-distribution text dropped performance by 3-16% absolute for most models. For direct models, random English words instead of the label space cost 5-16% absolute. Removing the input-label format was close to or worse than no demonstrations. With channel models, 75-87% of the gain was kept by pairing real inputs with random words.
quote: keeping the format of the input-label pairs is key
limits: 2022 models; classification and multiple choice; Direct MetaICL was an exception, attributed to meta-training.
agent_relevance: If an agent's few-shot exemplars mainly set format, in-context outcome history is a weak way to learn validity; keep a task-class counter in the harness (supports K07 and gap 5).
